title.en: Sikuliarsiujuitsok: The Giant Tied by His Feet
title.zh: 西庫利亞修尤伊特索克：縛足而亡的巨人

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale from Labrador, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 102 'A Tale from Labrador', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Too big to walk on new ice, Sikuliarsiujuitsok caught a whale from his kayak all by himself — dreaded and hated, never sleeping in strange places until persuaded into a snow-hut where, too big for room, he lay doubled up and let his feet be tied. Hauled out and killed — but not before killing four men in the struggle. His three sisters, one with three powerful sons, kept a stone-fenced enclosure into which they enticed all those they intended to kill.
summary.zh: 因身量過大而無法踏上新冰的西庫利亞修尤伊特索克，竟能獨自以皮艇捕鯨——人人畏懼憎恨，他從不在生地過夜；直到被勸入雪屋，體大難容、蜷縮而臥，任人縛住雙足。他被拖出殺害——臨死猶擊斃四人。他的三個姊妹（其一有三個強悍的兒子）築起石圍，專用來誘殺仇人。

passages.text: Sikuliarsiujuitsok, on account of his great size, was unable to walk upon new ice; he all by himself caught a whale from his kayak. But he was much dreaded and hated, and never ventured to sleep in strange places — he was however once persuaded to stay for a night in a snow-hut; being too big to find room in it he lay all doubled up, and allowed his feet to be tied together. In this condition he was hauled out and killed, but not before he himself had killed four men in the struggle. He had three sisters, one of whom had three sons likewise powerful men; they had an enclosure fenced in with stones into which they enticed all those they intended to kill.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 102 'A Tale from Labrador'; not verbatim.

title.en: Aklaujak: Drowning the Reindeer by the Antlers
title.zh: 阿克勞雅克：執角溺鹿的力士

region.en: Reindeer lakes and the lookout hill, Labrador
region.zh: 拉布拉多的馴鹿湖與瞭望山

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale from Labrador, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 103 'Aklaujak, a Tale from Labrador', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Of immense strength, Aklaujak returns from a reindeer-hunt to find his brothers have robbed him of his wife — but his mother, watching from a high hill as he sits in his kayak seizing two large reindeers by the antlers and drowning them by holding them under water, hastens down and persuades the wife to return to him, on which the brothers take flight.
summary.zh: 力大無窮的阿克勞雅克獵鹿歸來，發現兄弟們搶走了他的妻子；而他的母親在高山上望見他坐在皮艇中，雙手執住兩頭大鹿的鹿角、按入水中將其溺斃——她急忙下山勸妻子回到他身邊；兄弟們見狀倉皇而逃。

passages.text: A man named Aklaujak was of immense strength. Once, when away on a reindeer-hunt, his brothers robbed him of his wife; but the mother, who from a high hill observed him sitting in his kayak and seizing two large reindeers by the antlers and drowning them by holding them under water, hastened down and persuaded the wife to return to him, on which the brothers took flight.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 103 'Aklaujak, a Tale from Labrador'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Giant of Kangersuak: The Marshy Plain
title.zh: 康格蘇克的巨人與沼澤平原

region.en: Kangersuak or Cape Farewell, South Greenland
region.zh: 南格陵蘭康格蘇克（費爾韋爾角）

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 104 'The Giant of Kangersuak or Cape Farewell', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: At war, the northern people's powerful champion sat on the top of Kangersuak watching the Southlanders passing by. A man he had killed left a son who practised angakok science and revenged his father by inducing the giant to walk with him over a marshy plain, where he went down — and from beneath pierced the feet of the giant, and afterwards killed him.
summary.zh: 兩族交戰，北方人的強悍冠軍坐鎮康格蘇克山頂，專候過往的南方人。被他殺害的一人遺下一子，修習巫術，誘巨人與他同走沼澤平原——巨人陷入沼中，他自水底刺穿巨人的雙足，再將其擊斃，為父報仇。

passages.text: The people from the south (or east) and those from the north (or west) were at war with each other; the latter had a powerful champion who was sitting on the top of Kangersuak to watch the Southlanders passing by. A man who had been killed by him left a son, who practised angakok science and revenged his father by inducing the giant to walk with him over a marshy plain, where he went down — and from beneath pierced the feet of the giant, and afterwards killed him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 104 'The Giant of Kangersuak or Cape Farewell'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Kidnappers: The Magic Lay and the Dolphins' Speech
title.zh: 劫人者：咒歌與海豚之言

region.en: Coast of the girl and the gale

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 105 'The Kidnappers', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: A band of brothers tried to carry off a girl by force, but her mother by means of a magic lay caused them all to perish in a sudden gale. Some time after, an angakok who had been out kayaking stated that he had seen a shoal of dolphins — and listening to their speech made them out to be those brothers, who had been thus transformed.
summary.zh: 一夥兄弟企圖強搶少女，其母以咒歌召來驟風，令他們全數葬身海中；此後一名巫師出海時遇見一群海豚——聽其言語，正是那夥兄弟化為的形體。

passages.text: A band of brothers tried to carry off a girl by force; but her mother, by means of a magic lay, caused them all to perish in a sudden gale. Some time after an angakok who had been out kayaking stated that he had seen a shoal of dolphins, and listening to their speech made them out to be those brothers, who had been thus transformed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 105 'The Kidnappers'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Visiting Animals: Reindeer, Fox, and Hare

region.en: Lonely winter-house by the son's grave

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 106 'The Visiting Animals', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Grieving at his son's grave, an old man is surprised by three visitors: one tall and long-nosed, one smaller and flat-nosed, the last very small and white as snow — the flat-nosed one asking for a piece of sole-leather, the white one for a piece of walrus-tooth. Seeing the departing guests bound off in the shape of a reindeer, a fox, and a hare — it is said the hare had need of something for a new tooth.
summary.zh: 在兒子墳前守喪的老人，夜裡迎來三位客人：一個高挑長鼻、一個矮小塌鼻、最後一個瘦小而白如雪——臨別時，塌鼻者討走一塊皮底，白者討走一截海象牙。老人目送他們離去，驚見三人分別化作馴鹿、狐狸與野兔奔跳而去——據說那野兔正需要一件東西來換新牙。

passages.text: An old man, while staying in a firth to fish for salmon, lost his son, who died at some distance up the country; in his grief he could not persuade himself to leave his son's grave, and therefore put up his winter-house on the spot. In this lonely abode they were once surprised by seeing three men entering the house, one of them tall and long-nosed, the other smaller and with a flat nose, and the last of very small stature and white as snow. After passing the evening talking with the host the short-nosed man before starting asked for a piece of sole-leather, and the white one wanted a piece of walrus-tooth; the old man saw the departing visitors out, but when they left him stood dumfoundered at seeing them bounding off in the shape of a reindeer, a fox, and a hare — it is said that the hare had need of something for a new tooth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 106 'The Visiting Animals'; not verbatim.

title.en: Avigiatsiak: Taken by the Whale, Reborn from the Seal
title.zh: 阿維吉阿茨夏克：鯨奪豹生

region.en: Beach where the knife was ground

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 107 'Avigiatsiak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Grinding her knife on the beach, the young woman Avigiatsiak is taken by a whale; living for a time with the whales she flees and is transformed into a seal — caught, hauled upon the ice, cut to pieces all excepting the head thrown beneath the bench — from thence she slips into the womb of the man's wife who had harpooned her, and is afterwards born anew, and called Avigiatsiak.
summary.zh: 在海灘磨刀的少女阿維吉阿茨夏克被鯨擄走；與鯨同處一段時日後逃出，化身為海豹——被人叉獲、拖上冰面肢解，唯頭顱被拋於長凳之下——她自那裡鑽入叉她之人的妻子腹中，重生為人，仍名阿維吉阿茨夏克。

passages.text: Avigiatsiak was the name of a young woman who, while grinding her knife on the beach, was taken by a whale; after living for a time with the whales she fled and was transformed into a seal, living with the seals. As such she was caught by a man, hauled upon the ice, and cut to pieces, all excepting the head which was thrown beneath the bench — from thence she slipped into the womb of the man's wife who had harpooned her, and was afterwards born anew and called Avigiatsiak.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 107 'Avigiatsiak'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Bird's Cliff: The House of Black and White People

region.en: Fog-bound sea and the cave in the rock

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 108 'The Bird's Cliff', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Chased by a kayariak far off the land, father and son strike their persecutor dead from a flake of ice — but before sinking he spats repeatedly to all parts of the horizon, raising a dense fog that makes them wander. Landing at last, the angakok father perceives a house: one side inhabited by black people, the other by white ones; leaving after talk with both sides, they look back and see the house was a cave in the rock, the inhabitants gulls and ravens, and a drollish visitor staying with them, a falcon.
summary.zh: 父子在遠海被幽靈艇客追趕，自浮冰上將其擊斃——但那怪客沉海之前不斷向四方吐唾，霎時濃霧四起，父子迷失歸途。登岸後，身為巫師的父親覓得一屋：一側住著黑人，一側住著白人；與兩側居民交談作別後回望——那屋竟是巖中洞穴，居民原是海鷗與渡鴉，還有一位滑稽的訪客——獵隼。

passages.text: A father and his son, while kayaking far off the land, fell in with a kayariak who at once gave chase to them; they fortunately escaped by jumping out on a flake of ice, from which they struck their persecutor dead — but before sinking into the sea he spat repeatedly, turning round to all parts of the horizon, on which a dense fog arose causing them to wander and preventing their gaining their home. At last they reached land, and the father being angakok soon perceived a house and entered it — they found one side of it inhabited by black people and the other by white ones. After staying a while and having some talk with the inmates on both sides they left the house; but on looking behind them saw that the house was a cave in the rock, the inhabitants gulls and ravens, and a drollish visitor staying with them, a falcon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 108 'The Bird's Cliff'; not verbatim.

title.en: Kuanak: The Angakok Who Came Back from the Sea-Bottom
title.zh: 庫阿納克：自海底歸來的巫師

region.zh: 南格陵蘭的飛行之路與皮蘇格菲克

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 109 'Kuanak, an Angakok in South Greenland', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Head and feet tied for flight, Kuanak escapes the amarsiniook by dropping beneath sea and earth and emerging from his own house-floor; his drum soars of itself when he is found almost dying, an old kayak-cover having frightened him into his fall. Capsized by his own harpooned seal, he wakes at the sea-bottom with his grandmother, who ties his jacket close and pushes him up in a piece of skin — three landings scare him off (a urine-tub, a woman dressing her hair), the third fright would have lost him to the living for ever; at Pisugfik two dice-playing old men touch him senseless and chant him back, and his relatives, mourning-days done, hear his song from the boat that brings him home.
summary.zh: 縛首縛足而飛的庫阿納克，自山中竄出的阿馬爾西尼奧克魔掌下躍海而逃——穿海床、穿地底，從自家地板浮出；他的神鼓自行飛舞，而他幾乎凍斃於雪地——嚇他的是一張舊皮艇罩。被自己叉中的海豹掀翻後，他在海底醒來，祖母替他縛緊外套、以一塊皮為艇送他上升；三次登岸皆受驚逃（一盆尿、一個梳髮的女子），第三次若再受驚便永無生還之機——在皮蘇格菲克，兩個擲骰的老人觸他昏厥又以咒歌喚醒，送他還鄉；喪期已滿、幾已將他遺忘的親人，聽見送他回村的舟上唱起了庫阿納克的歌。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale per Rink; documents anghiniartok revival at Pisugfik (compare tale 79).

passages.text: Kuanak, an Angakok in South Greenland, started for a flight, having previously had his feet and his head tied together; while passing along between two high rocks an amarsiniook rushed out from the mountain-side and wanted to take him into his hood — he made his escape by dropping into the sea, and proceeding onwards beneath the surface of the sea and the earth finally emerged from the floor of his own house. Another time when he had gone off on a flight his drum, which he had left in the house, was lifted up by itself and soared about in the room till at length it stopped and fell down; at that same moment a voice was heard from without, and hastening to look whence it came they found him in an almost dying state lying upon the snow, an old skin-cover from a kayak having frightened him and caused his downfall.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 109 'Kuanak, an Angakok in South Greenland'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Kuanak was once capsized by a seal he had just harpooned; but being an anghiniartok his senses again returned, and he found himself at the bottom of the sea in company with his grandmother — she tied his kayak-jacket close to his body leaving no part of it uncovered, and then supplying him with a piece of skin by way of kayak pushed him upwards. When he emerged from the water he first betook himself far out to sea and thence made the land again, but happened to touch at an inhabited place where somebody was emptying out the urine-tub which scared him away from the shore — he tried to land on another place, but here a woman dressing her hair on the beach scared him away; if he had a third time taken fright he would never have returned to the land of the living.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 109 'Kuanak, an Angakok in South Greenland'; not verbatim.

passages.text: But he happened to land at Pisugfik where a couple of old men were sitting playing at dice — they at once knew him to be an anghiniartok, and on merely touching his naked body he dropped down senseless; but on their chanting a magic lay he revived. They then brought him back to his homestead, where his relatives, who had already finished their days of mourning and nearly forgotten him, were gladly surprised at hearing the crew of the boat that brought him home intuning Kuanak's song.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 109 'Kuanak, an Angakok in South Greenland'; not verbatim.

title.en: An Angakok on Kekertarsuak: The Funeral Kayak-Cover
title.zh: 凱克爾塔舒亞克的巫師：喪用艇罩

region.zh: 已婚姊妹所居的凱克爾塔舒亞克島

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 110 'An Angakok on Kekertarsuak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: His dogs stop dead before his sister's house; inside, all the people lie lifeless, eyes open and staring — his sister alone creeps towards him chewing, mouth widely opened as if to devour him, and the dogs start at the last moment. A conjuration and an angakok flight examine the place: those people had been frightened to death by the sight of a skin-cover from a kayak, which had been used at a funeral to carry the corpse upon.
summary.zh: 犬隊在妹妹的屋前僵立不前；屋內之人橫躺直坐、圓睜雙目、氣息全無——唯有妹妹蠕動著嘴如咀嚼狀，大張著口向他爬來，犬隊在最後關頭方才驚起。巫師歸家降神、飛往勘察：那些人都是被一張皮艇罩嚇死的——那正是喪禮上用來抬屍的艇罩。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale per Rink; mass fright-death documented.

passages.text: An Angakok on Kekertarsuak set off in his sledge to visit his married sister; on approaching the house his dogs suddenly stopped. After in vain trying to urge them on with his whip he alighted and went up to the house on foot — but seeing no people about he looked in at the window, and was horror-struck at seeing all the people lying or sitting about lifeless, their eyes open and staring. His sister alone showed signs of life, and seeing her brother began to move her mouth as if chewing, and crept towards the entrance; at sight of this he was struck with terror and fled to his dogs, but was again unable to make them stir — not until the sister had come quite close, her mouth widely opened as if to devour him, did they suddenly start, and thus he escaped to his home. Afterwards he performed a conjuration and undertook an angakok flight to examine the place — on his return he reported that those people had been frightened to death by the sight of a skin-cover from a kayak (viz., which had been used at a funeral to carry the corpse upon).
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 110 'An Angakok on Kekertarsuak'; not verbatim.

title.en: Singajuk and His Descendants: Mangilak, Baptised Moses
title.zh: 辛亞尤克家世：受洗名摩西的曼吉拉克

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 111 'Singajuk and his Descendants', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: A miscarried child swaddled in eider-duck skin, fostered with the utmost care to keep it alive, Mangilak becomes one of the most powerful of men — his first deed killing an ingnersuak. Caught in a gale, he learns a calm-spell by listening to a gull swimming in a solitary patch of smooth water, and from that time was not to be equalled in kayaking. Widowed, he visits his wife's grave and talks with the deceased, who gives him a mussel-shell containing a drink to endow him with angakok wisdom; he married again, and his son Akajarok died a Christian, while Mangilak himself, baptised and named Moses, was too full of angakok wisdom to become more than a nominal Christian.
summary.zh: 一個流產的嬰孩被裹在絨鴨皮中、悉心哺育才得存活——曼吉拉克長成為最強悍的人之一，首功便是誅殺一名地下精靈。海上遇風暴時，他聽著靜水窪中泅游的海鷗之聲習得止風咒，從此划艇無人能敵。喪妻後他常去墳前與亡妻交談，她以貝殼盛來一杯賦予巫智的飲液；再娶得子，其孫女正是講述此故事者之祖母。其子阿卡亞洛克以基督徒身分离世；曼吉拉克自己受洗名摩西，卻因巫智太深，始終只是個掛名的基督徒。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale with genealogical frame (the narrator's own ancestor); Christian syncretism noted in the source.

passages.text: Singajuk was a celebrated hunter living in Kangek (near Godthaab); his wife miscarried and brought forth a poor little wretch of a child that was swaddled in the skin of an eider-duck, and had to be fostered with the utmost care to keep it alive — this child was called Mangilak, and became one of the most powerful of men. His first deed was killing an ingnersuak; afterwards he was once caught in a gale of wind at sea, but espying a solitary spot of smooth water and a gull swimming in it, by dint of listening to its voice he learned a spell for procuring a calm, and from that time he was not to be equalled in kayaking.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 111 'Singajuk and his Descendants'; not verbatim.

passages.text: His mother then persuaded him to marry, and he took a wife who however shortly afterwards died; being almost a wizard he used to visit her grave and talk with the deceased, and on one occasion she gave him a mussel-shell containing a drink to endow him with angakok wisdom. Mangilak married a second wife and got a son called Akajarok, whose daughter became the grandmother of the man who related this story (to the author); Akajarok died a Christian — Mangilak also was baptised and named Moses, but was too full of angakok wisdom to become more than a nominal Christian.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 111 'Singajuk and his Descendants'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Cousins: The Toolik's Red-Hot Weapon
title.zh: 表兄弟：托洛克之赤熱兇器

region.en: The enemies' house and the flying angakok
region.zh: 仇家之屋與飛行的巫師

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 112 'The Cousins', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Like tale 15 but with the revenge brought on by an angakok who assisted the cousins on a flight: staying with them he invoked his tornak the toolik, who carried a red-hot weapon and destroyed the house and all its inhabitants by fire while the angakok flew homewards. Narrating the deed to his people, a laughing voice was heard from without, recognised as that of his erkungasok (the ingenious and cunning adviser, but rather powerless and boasting dweller among the tornaks), come to give notice of his having also assisted at the destruction of his enemies.
summary.zh: 與故事十五同型，但復仇由巫師促成：他在飛行中陪伴表兄弟，召來手持赤熱兇器的靈助托洛克——趁巫師飛回之際，一把火燒燬仇家之屋及其全部居民。歸家講述戰果時，屋外傳來笑聲——那是他的厄爾孔加索克（靈助中足智多謀卻無甚本事、慣於自誇的傢伙）——特地前來表功：那場火他也有份。

passages.text: This tale is somewhat similar to No. 15, but in the present version the revenge is brought on by an angakok who assisted the cousins on a flight; while staying with them he invoked his tornak the toolik, who carried a red-hot weapon and destroyed the house and all its inhabitants by fire while the angakok flew homewards. After his return to his house while narrating the deed to his people a laughing voice was heard from without, recognised as that of his erkungasok (the ingenious and cunning adviser, but rather powerless and boasting dweller among the tornaks), who came to give notice of his having also assisted at the destruction of his enemies.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 112 'The Cousins'; not verbatim.

title.en: Manik: The Boat-Crew of Rowing Girls
title.zh: 馬尼克：一船划槳的姑娘

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 113 'Manik', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: A bachelor till the day he suddenly ordered his mother to make ready the boat: he carried away the chief hunter's daughter crying and struggling in vain, pushed off north with all speed, and at every inhabited place carried away another woman — until he had got a complete boat's crew of rowing girls. Wintering in the far north he had an adventurous meeting with the ghost of a deceased woman, and found people feasting upon various meats hauled from the ground by magic lays; next year he returned all the women to their relatives excepting the first one, kept for his wife.
summary.zh: 孑然一身的馬尼克忽然命母親備船：他搶走大獵手的女兒——她哭喊掙扎皆屬徒勞——飛速北去；途經每一處村落便再搶一名女子，直到湊齊一船划槳的姑娘。遠北過冬時，他奇遇一名亡婦之魂，又見一屋之人以咒歌自地底拉出各色肉食宴飲；翌年南歸，他把女子們一一送還親屬，只留下第一個作為妻子。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale; abduction presented as told in the 1875 source.

passages.text: Manik was a great seal-hunter, but his mother in vain urged him to take a wife; he continued a bachelor till one day he suddenly ordered his mother to make ready the boat for removing from the place. As soon as she had made all ready he hastened up to the house of the chief hunter, who at the time was absent, and carried away his daughter, crying and struggling in vain to be released. Having placed her on the boat he at once pushed off and made for the north with all speed; at the first inhabited place they came past he again carried away a woman, and this continued until he had got a complete boat's crew of rowing girls.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 113 'Manik'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He continued his voyage the whole season till at length, having reached the far north, the frost set in and for the time obliged him to take up his quarters there; while wintering here and making excursions into the country he once came to a solitary house where he had an adventurous meeting with the ghost of a deceased woman, and from there came to another where he found the people feasting upon various meats which they kept hauling from the ground by help of magic lays. The next year he set out for his own country, returning to their relatives all the women excepting only the first one, whom he kept for his wife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 113 'Manik'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Land of the Isarukitsok Bird

region.en: The sunken promontory south of Godthaab
region.zh: 努克以南已沉沒的海岬

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; a story from South Greenland, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 114 'The Land of the Isarukitsok Bird', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Lost in fog, three kayakers come to a high promontory of one continuous steep inaccessible cliff inhabited by crowds of isarukitsoks (the great auk); resting and filling their kayaks with birds, they put off again and pass by one of the monstrous gulls which are in the habit of picking up kayakers and giving them as food to their young ones — but reach home in safety. Before the land of the isarukitsok sank, there were plenty of these birds about Nook (Godthaab).
summary.zh: 霧中迷航的三名皮艇客，來到一道綿延陡峭、人不可攀的海岬——其上棲滿大海雀；他們飽餐海鳥、滿載皮艇而歸，途中經過一隻慣於抓起皮艇客餵雛的巨鷗——幸而平安到家。據說在大海雀之鄉沉沒之前，努克一帶這種鳥還很多。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale; the great auk (Pinguinus impennis) extinction is embedded in the legend.

passages.text: Two young men with one elder companion lost their way when kayaking in foggy weather, and having roamed about without being able to sight any land came to a high promontory, showing one continuous steep and inaccessible cliff, inhabited by crowds of isarukitsoks. By following the coast they at last came to a landing-place, and found a nice situation where they rested themselves and had their strength restored by eating birds — having also filled their kayaks with them they put off to sea again, and happened to pass by one of the monstrous gulls which are in the habit of picking up the kayakers and giving them as food to their young ones; but they reached their home in safety. It is told that before the land of the isarukitsok sank there were plenty of these birds about Nook (Godthaab).
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 114 'The Land of the Isarukitsok Bird'; not verbatim.
